What has been built, and what the evidence supports
ShelfSense converts a planogram into a frozen audit reference, processes a shelf photograph, and produces an explainable compliance report.
Planogram designer stores shelf geometry in centimetres and prevents overlap or out-of-bounds placement.
Image pipeline detects shelf elements, extracts product crops, maps rows and positions, then matches only the shelf-scoped catalogue.
Compliance report preserves evidence, locations, confidence gates, and operator dispositions.
10 low-confidence boxes withheld from identity and quantity decisions
A shelf photo contains visual evidence. A planogram contains physical expectations. Compliance requires a defensible comparison.
A detector can locate packaging without proving the exact catalogue identity.
Rows and x-positions in pixels must align with an expected physical shelf layout.
Lookalike packaging, occlusion, perspective, and low-confidence detections must remain reviewable rather than turn into false alerts.
Claim “missing” or “misplaced” only when identity and calibrated position support it.

Each processing job captures the planogram state and the relevant shelf catalogue before analysis begins
Shelf width, rows, product placements, facings
The matcher excludes unrelated catalogue products captured outside the selected shelf.
It preserves the actual candidate set that existed when the audit started.
It makes a weak visual match an explicit review state rather than a confident global-catalogue guess.
Shelf parsing, row understanding, and cutout extraction
YOLO weights detect product / empty-space and shelf-row evidence. Product detection and exact identity remain separate tasks.
Segments shelf rows, detects product and empty-space proposals, filters product crops below 0.60 confidence, and retains excluded boxes as uncertainty geometry.
Important boundary: a bounding box proves location, not the exact SKU or variant.
Exact catalogue matching uses crop-level evidence. Cluster consensus helps repeated shelf items but does not replace per-crop identity.

Use the frozen shelf catalogue only.
Color compatibility filters candidates first.
Compare crop embedding with packshot embeddings using CLIP cosine similarity.
Accept only when score and margin clear provisional thresholds. Otherwise keep reviewable.
Consolidate only a clear same-row catalogue majority. Preserve individual matches.
CLIP score 0.90 and ambiguity margin 0.03 are present in code but require controlled crop-level calibration. No trained YOLO SKU-classifier or variant accuracy metric is claimed.
Planogram coordinate mapping and compliance decisions
The audit compares expected facing slots with observed, calibrated crop positions in the same row coordinate system
15 expected facings per row  |  width 120 cm  |  top-to-bottom row index
Conservative rule: when calibration is unavailable, the audit reports “needs review” instead of inferring a definitive missing-stock result.
The frontend persists planograms and image-processing outputs through the FastAPI backend
The designer uses a dark SaaS shell, hierarchy outliner, physical shelf canvas, and direct API synchronization. The analysis flow renders cutout and compliance evidence in the same application.

The fixture provides scenario-level acceptance rules. It does not establish detector precision, recall, or calibrated measurement accuracy.
Regression target: report one misplaced Lays on Row 1 and one empty Lays facing on Row 2 without false low-stock alerts.
Tests exercise the isolated backend, image parser, frontend behavior, and critical browser journeys
What these results do not prove
They confirm implemented behavior and regressions, not field accuracy, mAP, precision/recall, retail generalization, or OCR accuracy.

The project moved from layout design toward an evidence-conservative photo-to-planogram audit
Allows layout rules, exports, and compliance positions to use a common real-world coordinate system.
Prevents a later planogram edit from rewriting the expected state of an already processed shelf photo.
Reduces irrelevant lookalike candidates and preserves the job’s relevant product catalogue.
Uncalibrated position or weak identity evidence becomes review-needed, not a fabricated shortage or exact-SKU claim.
The prototype intentionally keeps uncertain evidence visible instead of overstating capability
No labelled real-shelf benchmark provides precision, recall, mAP, or SKU accuracy.
CLIP threshold and ambiguity margin are fixture-informed but not calibrated across product categories.
Perspective handling supports optional ArUco calibration; physical repeatability remains unmeasured.
Packshot embeddings and color gates can confuse visually similar packs and seasonal changes.
Live smoke test exists, but no labelled price-tag data supports accuracy claims.
Local SQLite, disk storage, and model dependencies suit prototype use rather than production scale.
The highest-value next step is measurable validation on a controlled physical shelf
Measured shelf rows, pixel boxes, exact SKU/variant identities, price labels, and multiple controlled error scenarios.
Measure detector quality, matching accuracy, position tolerance, empty-space recall, and OCR correctness.
Expand catalogue packshots, add variant-specific data, hard-negative examples, and human review feedback.
Move beyond local storage, define monitoring, access controls, deployment, and retailer workflow integration.
Mentor prompt: validate the controlled fixture design and success metrics before expanding model complexity.
